ctx: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell address to Israel, restating the covenant for a people about to enter the land. Chapter 19 sits in its legal core: cities of refuge for the man who kills without intent, a ban on moving a neighbor's boundary stone, and then the rule on witnesses. All three protect one thing, a community's ability to judge fairly when a life or a livelihood depends on what is said.

The text here is the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament read by Greek-speaking Jews and by the first Christians. Its wording matters for this series because the New Testament repeats the rule in terms that follow it closely.
inv: The rule is a limit on every single voice.

inv.q: One witness shall not stand to testify against a man for any iniquity, or for any fault, or for any sin which he may commit

inv: , and the sentence closes with the standard:

inv.q: by the mouth of two witnesses, or by the mouth of three witnesses, shall every word be established

inv: . Notice the word. Not every verdict: every word. A claim does not become true by being spoken with confidence. It becomes established when a second voice, not the first, says the same thing.
The law repeats itself because it was built to hold under pressure. It governs executions:

inv.q: He shall die on the testimony of two or three witnesses
one witness shall not testify against a soul that he should die

inv: . Then Deuteronomy 19 turns the rule around and guards the other side. If a witness brings a false charge,

inv.q: the judges shall make diligent inquiry

inv: , and a proved liar receives what he schemed for his brother:

inv.q: then shall ye do to him as he wickedly devised to do against his brother

inv: . False witness is not a private failing. It is a crime against the whole community, and it is punished with its own intended sentence.
Now watch what the New Testament does with the rule. Jesus gives it to the church as procedure:

inv.q: every word may be stood upon the testimony of two or three witnesses
On the mouth of two or three witnesses every word will be established

inv: . He gives it to Timothy for handling charges against leaders:

inv.q: Do not receive an accusation against an elder, except upon two or three witnesses

inv: . And Hebrews treats it as settled law:

inv.q: on the basis of two or three witnesses

inv: . None of them defends the rule. They assume it.

That is the rule behind this series. A witness here is not a quotation to admire. It is a voice that must be confirmed by another. Over the coming days we put the rule to work on Jesus, on an apostle's hearers, on a book most Bibles omit, and last of all on the apostles and angels themselves.

w: The same rule at the gravest stakes: no one is put to death on a single voice.
x.q: a man who is put to death shall not be put to death for one witness

w: The rule appears in the law of murder too, so it is not a quirk of one chapter.
x.q: one witness shall not testify against a soul that he should die

w: Jesus turns the rule into the church's procedure for a wrong between believers.
x.q: every word may be stood upon the testimony of two or three witnesses

w: Paul places his own coming visit under the rule.
x.q: On the mouth of two or three witnesses every word will be established

w: A New Testament writer treats the rule as established law and builds an argument on it.
x.q: dies without mercies on the basis of two or three witnesses

take: In Scripture no claim is established by one voice, however sure of itself. It is established when another voice confirms it.
